title: Say it twice, see who points
allegory: The induction score is a déjà vu test: read fifty nonsense words aloud twice, and on the second pass measure how often each listener points at the word that followed the current word last time.
map: a list of nonsense words read aloud twice
where each listener points during the second reading
the word that came right after this word's first appearance
the average share of pointing at that spot
the induction score: mean of that diagonal
a seating chart shaded by score
a layer × head heatmap whose bright cells are candidates

chapters.name: Which head is it?
chapters.note: 12 layers × 12 heads. where are the copiers?

cap.1: A model has over a hundred attention heads. Some of them spot repeats and copy. How do you find those without studying each one by hand?
cap.2: GPT-2 small has 12 layers of 12 heads. You want the induction heads among them. Rather than eyeballing 144 attention patterns, build one number per head that ranks them all.
cap.3: Candidate discovery at scale needs a cheap, mechanism-specific statistic computed for every head in one forward pass, followed by causal checks on the top scorers.

props.label: blick zorp fen ... | blick zorp fen ...

cap.1: Read fifty nonsense words aloud, then read them again. On the second pass some listeners point at the word that came next last time. Those are the copiers.
cap.2: Random tokens can't be predicted from meaning, only from repetition. Repeat them once and the second half becomes copyable: loss drops off a cliff there, and induction heads light up.
cap.3: A self-concatenated random sequence (50 tokens, twice, BOS prepended) isolates induction: bigram statistics are useless, so any second-half loss drop must come from in-context copying.

chapters.name: The stripe
chapters.title: an induction head on A B C D A B C D

cap.1: Each second-pass word points at the word after its first appearance. On the chart that makes a bright stripe parallel to the diagonal, one copy back.
cap.2: Rows are the token doing the looking, columns the token looked at. The induction stripe sits at offset 1 − seq_len: from each repeat to the token after its earlier twin.
cap.3: For destination i in the second copy, source = i − seq_len + 1, the successor of the previous occurrence. Offset −seq_len is the duplicate-token stripe; offset 0, a current-token head.

cap.1: Take one listener's pointing chart, read off the stripe, and average it. One number per head: near 1 means a copier, near 0 means not.
cap.2: pattern.diagonal(dim1=-2, dim2=-1, offset=1-seq_len).mean(), computed by a hook on every hook_pattern in one forward pass. Heads above roughly 0.4 are induction heads.
cap.3: Computed live via hooks on blocks.*.attn.hook_pattern, no full cache needed. In ARENA's 2L attention-only model heads 1.4 and 1.10 score above 0.6; nearly everything else sits near zero.

chapters.name: The glowing seats
chapters.title: induction score per head, ARENA's 2-layer model

cap.1: Shade every listener by score and two seats glow. They're your suspects. A glowing seat is a lead, not a verdict: next you check each one properly.
cap.2: In ARENA's 2-layer model heads 1.4 and 1.10 light up; on GPT-2 small the same detector flags 5.1, 5.5, 6.9, 7.2 and 7.10. Then zero-ablate each and watch second-half loss climb back.
cap.3: The score is correlational; confirm by ablation. The enabling previous-token head (0.7) scores near zero here, because its role is indirect: it tells 1.4 and 1.10 where to look.

chapters.name: One seat off

left.title: offset = 1 − seq_len
lines: the token after the earlier twin

chapters.verdict: seq_len is one copy, and BOS shifts every index by one.

cap.1: Check one seat too far back and you score a different kind of listener: the ones pointing at the earlier twin itself, not the word after it.
cap.2: offset = −seq_len scores duplicate-token heads; offset 0 scores current-token heads. Use the length of one copy, not the doubled sequence, and account for the BOS token.
cap.3: If circuitsvis clearly shows a stripe but the score is near zero, the offset is wrong, not the head. seq_len is the single-copy length; BOS shifts indices by one.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Guess a mechanism, build a detector
Heatmap first, then ablate the bright cells

cap.1: This is interpretability in miniature: guess what a part does, invent a cheap test, scan the whole model, then check the suspects properly.
cap.2: The same loop finds other heads later, such as name movers. Induction heads matter because they are a main driver of in-context learning, the model's use of its own context.
cap.3: Detector, heatmap, ablation: the loop scales from induction heads to the IOI circuit. Knowing which heads implement copying is a first handle for understanding and steering in-context behaviour.

coda.title: A B C D A B C D: tap cells to move where each word points

readouts.label: cells in the future (a causal head can't)
readouts.f: sum(G.map((row, i) => sum(row.map((v, j) => (j > i && v) ? 1 : 0))))

caption.1: This starts as a previous-token head. In the bottom four rows, move each lit cell to the word after its earlier twin and watch the induction score climb to 1.
caption.2: Rows point, columns are pointed at. Each score averages one offset over the second copy, with rows renormalised to sum to 1. Light a cell above the diagonal and the head is no longer causal.
caption.3: Offset 1 − n is induction, −n duplicate-token, 0 current-token, −1 previous-token. A head that splits its row splits its score, which is why real heads land between 0 and 1.

where_else: Finding name mover and S-inhibition heads in the IOI circuit with the same score-then-ablate loop
Previous-token and duplicate-token head detectors: the same diagonal trick at different offsets
Sweeping probes or SAE latents across layers: one number per component, then verify the bright ones

hamming.what: One number per attention head: its average attention along the induction stripe of a repeated random sequence.
hamming.when: When you need to find induction heads, or any head with a predictable pattern, across a whole model at once.
hamming.why: It turns eyeballing every attention pattern into a ranked heatmap, so careful causal checks can focus on a few candidates.

object.title: The stripe block
object.subtitle: One head's attention on A B C D A B C D as a block of bars, morphing from previous-token to induction.

cap.1: A previous-token head: every word points at the one just before it. A tight stripe hugging the diagonal. Induction score: zero.
cap.2: Offset −1 pattern. Its induction score at offset 1 − 4 is 0.
cap.3: Previous-token head: mass on (i, i−1). Necessary upstream of induction, but invisible to the induction score.

cap.1: Slide to an induction head. In the second copy each word now points at the word after its earlier twin: the stripe jumps back.
cap.2: Second-copy rows move to offset 1 − seq_len = −3.
cap.3: Induction: mass on (i, i − n + 1) for i ≥ n, the successor of the previous occurrence.

cap.1: From above, the stripe is one clean diagonal. Average its height over the second copy and you have the score: here, 1.
cap.2: The induction score is the mean along that diagonal: 1.0 for this pure head.
cap.3: score = mean(diag(A, 1 − n)) over the second copy; a pure induction head scores 1.

cap.1: Halfway: each second-copy word splits its pointing. The score reads 0.5. Real heads are rarely pure, and the score still ranks them.
cap.2: A mixed head scores between 0 and 1, which is why a threshold like 0.4 is used.
cap.3: Scores are continuous because heads distribute mass; thresholds (ARENA uses roughly 0.4) turn a ranking into candidates.

cap.1: In the first copy there is nothing to copy yet, so here those rows rest on the first position. Only the second copy counts toward the score.
cap.2: First-copy rows have no earlier twin; the score is read on the repeated half.
cap.3: Only second-copy destinations have a defined induction target, so they carry the signal.

predict.q: A head attends from each second-copy token to its earlier twin itself, not the token after. What does the induction score say?

options.t: Near zero: that's a duplicate-token head at offset −seq_len

predict.why: The induction stripe is one position later, at offset 1 − seq_len.

predict.q: Your heatmap is near zero everywhere, but circuitsvis shows a clear stripe. Most likely?

options.t: The offset is wrong: doubled seq_len, or BOS ignored
The model has no induction heads

predict.why: Trust the picture: fix the offset before doubting the head.

predict.q: Why use random tokens instead of ordinary text?

options.t: Random tokens can only be predicted by copying, so induction stands alone

predict.why: With real text, meaning and common word pairs also help; random repeats isolate in-context copying.

object.where: Any detector by template: define the pattern a mechanism must produce, score every part, then verify the top hits.
